package_info.package_versions: all published versions (since at least Dec 4, 2023)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages abuse the npm registry by distributing large, non-software media files (such as movies, videos, and eBooks) in violation of platform terms of service. While they do not contain traditional malware, they undermine the integrity and security of the software supply chain by using the registry as a file hosting service for pirated or unauthorized content, increasing the risk of copyright infringement and supply chain pollution.

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when the package is downloaded, installed, or inspected)
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (multiple .ts files, e.g., video1.ts, video2.ts)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Stores and distributes large video files (likely DVD/Blu-ray rips) as part of the package contents. These files are not used by any code in the package and serve only to distribute pirated media.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of large binary video files in a software package is highly unusual and not justified by any code functionality. Such files are typically unrelated to software development and indicate misuse of the package registry for unauthorized media distribution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard npm packages contain JavaScript/TypeScript code and, at most, small assets necessary for the software's operation. Including multi-gigabyte video files, especially without any code referencing them, violates both technical and policy expectations for package content.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may include small demo videos or images for documentation or UI testing, but never full-length movies or large media files unrelated to the package's function.
key_indicators: Multiple large .ts files (tens of MB each) in the package root directory
Total package size (~54.5 MB per package) far exceeds typical npm packages
No code in the package references or utilizes the media files
File naming patterns (e.g., video1.ts, video2.ts) suggest partitioned media distribution

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when the package is downloaded, installed, or inspected)
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (JSON files with timestamped Mandarin comments)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Stores large JSON files containing time-synced user comments, likely scraped from online video streaming platforms. These files are not referenced by any code in the package and are included solely to distribute unauthorized data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Including large datasets of user comments, especially those synchronized to video timestamps and written in Mandarin, is not expected in a code package. Their presence suggests the package is being used to distribute data scraped from streaming platforms, which is unauthorized and unrelated to software functionality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages do not include large, unrelated user comment datasets, especially not those extracted from third-party platforms. Such data is not required for typical software operation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages might include small sample data for testing or demonstration, but not full archives of user comments from streaming services.
key_indicators: Large JSON files with time-synced comments in the package root
No code in the package references or processes these comment files
File content includes Mandarin text and timestamped entries
Package size is significantly increased by the presence of these files

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads npm packages with large video (.ts) files and JSON comment files, using a naming scheme (wlwz-*) to denote sequence or partitioning of media content.
attack_chain.leads_to: Packages are made available for download via the npm registry, enabling the distribution of pirated or unauthorized media and associated data.

attack_chain.action: Users or automated scripts download all related packages (matching the wlwz-* naming pattern) to reconstruct the full movie or media content, including associated user comments.
attack_chain.leads_to: Circumvention of npm platform restrictions, potential copyright violations, and pollution of the software supply chain with non-software content.

behavioral_signatures: Packages containing large binary media files (.ts, .mp4, etc.) unrelated to any code functionality
Packages with minimal or no executable code but large non-code assets (e.g., video or comment files)
Packages with naming patterns indicating sequence or partitioning (e.g., wlwz-*, wlwz-2312, wlwz-2313, etc.)
file_indicators: *.ts files in the package root directory
Large (>50MB) JSON files containing time-synced comments
Packages with total size >50MB and minimal or no code files
Presence of multiple large binary or data files with no corresponding code references
network_indicators: No direct network indicators; distribution occurs via the npm registry itself
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Flag npm packages that contain large binary media files (such as .ts, .mp4) or large JSON datasets unrelated to code, especially when the total package size exceeds typical thresholds (e.g., >10MB). Look for packages with minimal or no code and naming patterns suggesting partitioned media distribution (e.g., wlwz-*). Automated scanning should inspect package contents for non-code assets, anomalous file types, and size outliers. Cross-reference file types and sizes with the absence of code references to these assets to reduce false positives.
